title: Dyslipidemia: Treat Cardiovascular Risk, Not the LDL Alone
bottomLine: Lipid treatment is based on overall cardiovascular risk, established atherosclerotic disease and high-risk conditions, not an isolated LDL value. Confirm secondary causes and use shared decision-making around statin benefit and tolerance.
recognize: Established ASCVD, diabetes, CKD and markedly elevated LDL can place patients in treatment groups even when calculated short-term risk is modest.
Premature ASCVD or very high LDL should raise suspicion for familial hypercholesterolemia.
differentiate: Hypertriglyceridemia and LDL-predominant dyslipidemia have different immediate risks; very high triglycerides raise pancreatitis concern.
A reported statin symptom should be evaluated rather than automatically labelling permanent intolerance.
assessment: Assess smoking, BP, diabetes, CKD, family history, pregnancy potential, diet, alcohol, medications and prior ASCVD.
workup: Use a fasting or nonfasting lipid profile as appropriate and check secondary causes when the pattern is unexpected or severe.
management: Use guideline-directed statin intensity for risk category and add non-statin therapy when indicated by residual risk or statin limitation.
Treat lifestyle and all modifiable risk factors together.
medicationSafety: Statins are avoided in pregnancy; review interacting drugs and investigate significant muscle symptoms when clinically indicated.
redFlags: Very high triglycerides with abdominal pain
Premature or recurrent ASCVD despite therapy
counselling: Explain absolute risk reduction and the role of long-term adherence.
followUp: Recheck lipids and adherence after treatment changes and periodically thereafter.
examTrap: Withholding indicated statin therapy because the LDL is only mildly elevated in a patient with established vascular disease.
oneLinePearl: Treat the patient's vascular risk, not just the laboratory number.

title: Chronic Coronary Disease: Is the Angina Stable?
bottomLine: Predictable exertional chest pressure relieved by rest can fit stable angina, but any new, accelerating, prolonged or rest pain must be treated as possible acute coronary syndrome until excluded.
recognize: Stable angina is reproducible with exertion or stress and improves with rest or antianginal therapy.
Dyspnea, epigastric discomfort or reduced exercise tolerance can be ischemic equivalents.
differentiate: Musculoskeletal, reflux and anxiety symptoms may mimic ischemia, but risk factors and exertional pattern matter.
A normal resting ECG does not exclude coronary disease.
assessment: Characterize pain, functional limitation, risk factors, prior CAD, medications and bleeding risk.
workup: Use ECG and evidence-based noninvasive testing matched to pretest probability and local access; urgent evaluation is required if ACS cannot be excluded.
management: Address antiplatelet therapy when indicated, lipid lowering, BP/smoking/diabetes control and antianginal treatment.
Refer for cardiology evaluation when symptoms are refractory, diagnosis is uncertain or high-risk disease is suspected.
medicationSafety: Nitrates can cause hypotension and must not be combined with recent PDE5 inhibitors.
counselling: Teach when to stop activity and seek emergency care rather than repeatedly self-treating worsening symptoms at home.
followUp: Track symptom burden, exercise tolerance and secondary-prevention adherence.
examTrap: Calling recurrent rest pain 'stable angina' because the patient has known CAD.
oneLinePearl: Stable angina is stable only when its pattern is stable.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society chronic coronary syndrome resources

title: Acute Coronary Syndrome: ECG and Troponin Are Time-Critical
bottomLine: Suspected ACS requires rapid ECG, serial troponin strategy and risk-based reperfusion/antithrombotic management. Do not delay emergency transfer for an outpatient workup when ACS is plausible.
recognize: Pressure-like chest discomfort, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea or ischemic equivalents may occur.
Older adults, women and people with diabetes may have less typical pain.
differentiate: ST-elevation MI requires immediate reperfusion pathway; NSTEMI/unstable angina require serial ECG/troponin and risk assessment.
Aortic dissection, PE and pericarditis are important dangerous alternatives.
assessment: Assess ABCs, hemodynamics, pain onset, bleeding risk, medication history, cocaine/stimulant use and contraindications to antithrombotic therapy.
workup: Obtain ECG promptly and repeat if symptoms evolve; use serial high-sensitivity troponin according to the local validated pathway.
management: Activate emergency reperfusion pathway for STEMI and provide guideline-directed antiplatelet/anticoagulant and secondary-prevention therapy according to diagnosis and bleeding risk.
medicationSafety: Do not give fibrinolysis when aortic dissection is suspected; check bleeding risk and medication interactions before antithrombotic therapy.
redFlags: ST elevation or dynamic ischemic change
counselling: After stabilization, address smoking, cardiac rehabilitation, medication adherence and emergency symptom recognition.
followUp: Ensure cardiology follow-up and medication reconciliation after discharge.
examTrap: Ruling out MI from one normal troponin obtained soon after symptom onset.
oneLinePearl: ACS is a serial assessment: ECG plus time-appropriate troponin, not one snapshot.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society acute coronary syndrome guidance

title: Syncope: Find the Dangerous Cause Before Calling It Vasovagal
bottomLine: Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion. The priority is identifying cardiac, hemorrhagic, thromboembolic or other dangerous causes before diagnosing benign vasovagal syncope.
recognize: Vasovagal syncope often has trigger/prodrome and rapid recovery.
Exertional syncope, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, family history of sudden death or injury without prodrome increases cardiac concern.
differentiate: Seizure often has prolonged postictal confusion or stereotyped motor activity; hypoglycemia, intoxication and falls without true LOC can mimic syncope.
assessment: Obtain event history from patient/witness, orthostatic vitals when safe, cardiac/neurologic exam, medication review and pregnancy/bleeding assessment when relevant.
workup: ECG is core testing; targeted labs/imaging depend on the presentation rather than routine broad panels or neuroimaging.
management: Urgently evaluate high-risk cardiac or hemorrhagic features; manage orthostatic/vasovagal causes with trigger and medication strategies when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha blockers, nitrates and QT-prolonging drugs can contribute.
counselling: Provide driving/work restrictions according to jurisdiction and risk.
followUp: Arrange rhythm monitoring or specialty evaluation when intermittent arrhythmia remains plausible.
examTrap: Ordering a CT head routinely for uncomplicated syncope with no trauma or focal neurologic findings.
oneLinePearl: Syncope plus exertion or an abnormal ECG is cardiac until proven otherwise.

title: Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardia: Stable or Unstable?
bottomLine: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia is managed first by hemodynamic stability. Unstable tachycardia needs synchronized cardioversion; stable re-entrant SVT can often be treated with vagal manoeuvres then adenosine when appropriate.
recognize: SVT commonly presents with abrupt-onset rapid regular palpitations, lightheadedness, dyspnea or chest discomfort.
differentiate: Atrial fibrillation is usually irregular; sinus tachycardia has a physiologic driver and should not be suppressed without treating the cause.
Wide-complex tachycardia should be presumed ventricular until appropriately evaluated.
assessment: Assess BP, perfusion, ischemia, heart failure, oxygenation, medication/substance triggers and obtain a 12-lead ECG when possible.
workup: Check electrolytes, thyroid status or other precipitants when clinically indicated after acute stabilization.
management: Use synchronized cardioversion for instability; use vagal manoeuvres and guideline-directed acute therapy for stable regular SVT.
medicationSafety: Adenosine should not be used indiscriminately for irregular or polymorphic wide-complex rhythms and requires appropriate monitoring.
counselling: Teach trigger recognition and when recurrent symptoms require emergency evaluation.
followUp: Recurrent symptomatic SVT warrants rhythm documentation and consideration of electrophysiology referral.
examTrap: Treating sinus tachycardia from sepsis or hemorrhage as if it were re-entrant SVT.
oneLinePearl: Tachycardia treatment starts with stability and rhythm, then mechanism.

title: Bradycardia: Treat the Patient, Not the Rate
bottomLine: Bradycardia is dangerous when it causes poor perfusion or reflects high-grade conduction disease. Asymptomatic athletic sinus bradycardia is different from symptomatic AV block.
recognize: Symptoms include syncope/presyncope, hypotension, ischemic discomfort, heart failure or confusion.
Medication toxicity, ischemia, hyperkalemia, hypothyroidism and conduction-system disease are common causes.
differentiate: Sinus bradycardia retains P-QRS relationship; Mobitz II and complete heart block are higher-risk conduction disorders.
assessment: Assess perfusion and symptoms, obtain ECG and review beta blockers, non-DHP calcium channel blockers, digoxin and antiarrhythmics.
workup: Check electrolytes, ischemia and thyroid testing when relevant; use telemetry/rhythm monitoring for intermittent symptoms.
management: Symptomatic unstable bradycardia follows urgent chronotropic/pacing pathways while correcting reversible causes.
High-grade AV block warrants cardiology evaluation even if intermittently tolerated.
medicationSafety: Do not simply add another rate-slowing agent to a patient with unexplained bradycardia.
counselling: Review medications and driving/safety implications after syncope.
followUp: Arrange cardiology/pacemaker evaluation when conduction disease is persistent or symptomatic.
examTrap: Calling a heart rate of 45 automatically pathologic without assessing symptoms, rhythm and context.
oneLinePearl: Bradycardia becomes an emergency when perfusion fails or conduction disease is high risk.

title: Murmurs and Valve Disease: When the Sound Changes the Plan
bottomLine: A murmur matters when it suggests structural disease or accompanies symptoms. Syncope, exertional dyspnea, heart failure, cyanosis or a new murmur after infection/MI require more than reassurance.
recognize: Aortic stenosis classically causes exertional dyspnea, angina or syncope; mitral regurgitation can cause an apical holosystolic murmur and heart failure.
differentiate: Innocent childhood murmurs are typically soft and occur in an otherwise well child with normal growth, pulses and oxygenation.
A new murmur with fever raises infective endocarditis; a new murmur after MI can signal mechanical complication.
assessment: Assess timing, location, radiation, intensity, pulses, BP, JVP, heart failure signs and symptoms with exertion.
workup: Obtain echocardiography when structural disease is suspected or symptoms/signs warrant it.
management: Refer significant valve disease to cardiology and manage heart failure/arrhythmia complications while awaiting definitive intervention.
medicationSafety: Avoid aggressive preload reduction in severe fixed outflow obstruction when the patient is unstable.
counselling: Explain activity and dental/infection recommendations based on the confirmed lesion, not the presence of any murmur.
followUp: Valve severity and symptoms determine echocardiographic surveillance and referral timing.
examTrap: Giving antibiotic prophylaxis for routine dental work to every patient with a murmur.
oneLinePearl: A murmur is a clue; symptoms and structural diagnosis determine risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society valvular heart disease resources

title: Pericarditis and Myocarditis: Chest Pain Beyond ACS
bottomLine: Pleuritic positional chest pain with diffuse ECG changes can suggest pericarditis, while myocarditis may present with chest pain, arrhythmia or heart failure after infection. Both still require exclusion of ACS and assessment for hemodynamic compromise.
recognize: Pericarditis pain often improves sitting forward; myocarditis may cause troponin elevation, ventricular dysfunction or arrhythmia.
differentiate: Regional ischemic ECG changes and coronary-pattern symptoms favour ACS; tamponade physiology changes pericarditis from routine to emergent.
assessment: Assess recent infection, autoimmune disease, medications, hemodynamics, JVP, heart sounds and heart failure.
workup: Use ECG, troponin, inflammatory markers and echocardiography; further cardiac imaging or specialty testing is selected based on severity.
management: Uncomplicated pericarditis uses anti-inflammatory therapy when appropriate; myocarditis with arrhythmia or ventricular dysfunction requires cardiology and activity restriction.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs may be inappropriate in significant kidney disease, GI bleeding risk or some heart-failure contexts.
counselling: Avoid strenuous exercise until myocarditis has been appropriately evaluated and cleared.
followUp: Cardiology follow-up is needed for myocardial involvement or recurrent pericarditis.
examTrap: Assuming a positive troponin always means atherosclerotic MI.
oneLinePearl: Troponin identifies myocardial injury; the clinical syndrome tells you why.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society inflammatory heart disease practice resources

title: Infective Endocarditis: Culture Before Antibiotics When Safe
bottomLine: Persistent fever with bacteremia risk, prosthetic material, injection drug use or embolic phenomena should raise concern for endocarditis. Obtain appropriate blood cultures before antibiotics when the patient is stable enough, but never delay treatment of septic shock.
recognize: Fever, new/change in murmur, embolic stroke, splenic pain, skin/eye findings or persistent bacteremia can occur.
differentiate: A murmur is not required; culture-negative endocarditis exists, especially after prior antibiotics.
assessment: Assess prosthetic valves/devices, prior endocarditis, congenital heart disease, injection practices, recent bacteremia/procedures and embolic symptoms.
workup: Obtain multiple blood-culture sets and echocardiography; transesophageal imaging is often needed when suspicion remains high or prosthetic material is present.
management: Hospitalize suspected significant disease for IV antimicrobial and infectious-disease/cardiology management; evaluate for embolic and valve complications.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric antibiotics before cultures in a stable patient when cultures can be obtained immediately; do not delay antibiotics in shock.
counselling: Harm-reduction and substance-use care should be offered without stigma when injection-related infection is possible.
followUp: Ensure definitive treatment duration, repeat cultures and valve/device follow-up are coordinated.
examTrap: Waiting for a new murmur before considering endocarditis in a high-risk patient with persistent bacteremia.
oneLinePearl: Endocarditis is a bacteremia-plus-context diagnosis; the murmur may be absent.
sourceBasis: Canadian infectious disease and cardiology practice resources

title: Peripheral Arterial Disease: Claudication or Threatened Limb?
bottomLine: Exertional calf pain relieved by rest suggests claudication, but sudden pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis or poikilothermia suggests acute limb ischemia and needs emergency vascular care.
recognize: PAD is strongly associated with smoking, diabetes, CKD and systemic atherosclerosis.
differentiate: Neurogenic claudication is posture-dependent and may improve with flexion; venous disease produces edema/heaviness rather than reproducible ischemic exertional pain.
assessment: Assess pulses, skin, wounds, temperature, capillary refill, neurologic status and cardiovascular risk factors.
workup: Use ankle-brachial index for stable suspected PAD when valid; vascular imaging is indicated for threatened limb or intervention planning.
management: Use smoking cessation, exercise therapy, antiplatelet/statin therapy and risk-factor control; urgent vascular assessment for rest pain, tissue loss or acute ischemia.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic choices depend on bleeding risk and the confirmed vascular indication.
redFlags: Six Ps of acute limb ischemia
counselling: Foot care is especially important in diabetes and PAD.
followUp: Monitor walking limitation, wounds and vascular risk-factor control.
examTrap: Scheduling an outpatient ABI for a cold pulseless painful leg with neurologic deficit.
oneLinePearl: Acute limb ischemia is a limb emergency; do not send it to routine vascular testing.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society vascular prevention principles

title: Aortic Disease: Aneurysm Surveillance vs Dissection Emergency
bottomLine: Stable aneurysm is a surveillance and risk-factor problem; abrupt severe chest/back/abdominal pain with pulse or neurologic asymmetry is possible dissection and requires emergency aortic imaging and surgical/vascular care.
recognize: AAA risk rises with age, smoking and vascular disease; dissection risk rises with hypertension and connective-tissue/aortic disorders.
differentiate: Dissection can mimic ACS or stroke and may occur without the classic tearing description.
assessment: Assess pain onset/maximality, pulse/BP differences, neurologic deficits, aortic regurgitation signs and perfusion.
workup: Use urgent CT angiography or appropriate alternative imaging for suspected acute aortic syndrome; stable AAA surveillance depends on measured diameter and local pathway.
management: Suspected dissection requires emergency transfer, analgesia and carefully controlled hemodynamics under acute-care protocols.
Stable aneurysm requires smoking cessation and vascular referral/surveillance based on size and growth.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation or fibrinolysis given for presumed ACS can be catastrophic if aortic dissection is the true diagnosis.
counselling: Teach emergency symptoms and smoking cessation for known aneurysm.
followUp: Ensure imaging surveillance is not lost to follow-up.
examTrap: Giving fibrinolysis for chest pain with neurologic deficit and pulse asymmetry before considering dissection.
oneLinePearl: Chest pain plus pulse or neurologic asymmetry is an aortic emergency until excluded.
sourceBasis: Canadian vascular and cardiovascular practice resources

title: Orthostatic Hypotension: Medication, Volume, or Autonomic?
bottomLine: Orthostatic symptoms are a physiology problem, not simply a low standing BP. Identify volume depletion, medication effects and autonomic disease, then treat the cause while reducing falls and syncope risk.
recognize: Lightheadedness, blurred vision, weakness or syncope after standing is typical; older adults and people with Parkinson disease, diabetes or polypharmacy are at higher risk.
differentiate: Vertigo is an illusion of movement; orthostatic presyncope is cerebral hypoperfusion.
Postural tachycardia and orthostatic hypotension are different hemodynamic syndromes.
assessment: Measure orthostatic vitals correctly when safe, review fluids, bleeding/GI losses, antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates and autonomic symptoms.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes, ECG or endocrine testing only when the clinical context suggests anemia, volume/electrolyte loss, arrhythmia or adrenal disease.
management: Correct volume depletion, rationalize contributing medication and use physical countermeasures; pharmacotherapy is reserved for persistent symptomatic cases after cause-directed measures.
medicationSafety: Overtreating supine hypertension can worsen orthostatic symptoms; pressor drugs can worsen supine hypertension.
counselling: Teach slow position changes, hydration strategies when appropriate and falls precautions.
followUp: Reassess symptoms after medication or volume changes rather than targeting a number alone.
examTrap: Adding a pressor drug before reviewing the patient's diuretic and alpha-blocker regimen.
oneLinePearl: Orthostasis often starts in the medication list.
sourceBasis: Canadian geriatrics and cardiovascular practice principles
